details:
**Io and the gadfly**
Io was a mortal lover of Zeus whom he turned into a white heifer to hide her from Hera. Hera claimed the cow, set the hundred-eyed (or thousand-eyed) giant Argus Panoptes to guard her, and later sent a gadfly to sting her and drive her across the world.

**Peacock and the eyes of Argus**
After Hermes killed Argus to free Io, Hera placed Argus's many eyes on the tail feathers of her sacred bird, the peacock. Peacocks also pull her chariot.

**Tiresias**
The Theban seer, whom Hera turned into a woman after he struck a pair of mating snakes with a stick. Years later, Zeus and Hera asked him whether men or women enjoy sex more; when he answered women, Hera blinded him, and Zeus compensated him with prophecy.

**Judgment of Paris**
When Eris's golden apple marked "to the fairest" sparked a contest among Hera, Athena, and Aphrodite, the Trojan prince Paris served as judge. Hera offered him kingship over all of Europe and Asia, but he chose Aphrodite, who offered him Helen.

**Ixion and Nephele**
The Lapith king Ixion tried to seduce or rape Hera, so Zeus formed a cloud in her likeness, Nephele. Ixion slept with the cloud, fathering Centaurus (ancestor of the centaurs), and was punished by being bound to an eternally spinning fiery wheel in Tartarus.

**Serpents in Heracles's cradle**
Jealous of Zeus's son by Alcmene, Hera sent two snakes to kill the infant Heracles, who strangled them. She persecuted him all his life, sending monsters such as the Nemean Lion and the Hydra and driving him mad so that he killed his own children, until he became a god and she gave him her daughter Hebe as a wife.

**Lamia**
A Libyan queen loved by Zeus. Hera killed her children (or drove her to kill them) and cursed her with sleeplessness, turning her into a monster who devours other people's children.

**Cleobis and Biton**
Two sons of Cydippe, a priestess of Hera at Argos, who pulled their mother's cart to Hera's festival when no oxen were available. When Cydippe prayed for the best gift a mortal could receive, Hera let them die peacefully in their sleep, a story told by Herodotus.

**Galanthis and Eurystheus**
Hera delayed Heracles's birth by having Eileithyia, goddess of childbirth, sit with her limbs crossed outside Alcmene's room, and she hastened the birth of Eurystheus so he would rule over Heracles. Alcmene's servant Galanthis tricked Eileithyia into releasing the spell, and Hera turned Galanthis into a weasel.

**Milky Way**
Hera was tricked into nursing the infant Heracles, and when she pulled him away from her breast, the spilled milk sprayed across the sky to form the Milky Way.

**Cuckoo**
Zeus won Hera by disguising himself as a bedraggled cuckoo in a storm. Hera took pity and held the bird to her breast, and Zeus resumed his true form and ravished her; the story is set on Mount Thornax.

**Hephaestus and the golden throne**
Hera threw her son Hephaestus off Olympus because he was lame or ugly. In revenge he sent her a golden throne that trapped her, and he released her only after Dionysus got him drunk and brought him back to Olympus.

**Hung from the sky with golden chains**
In the Iliad, Zeus punished Hera for raising a storm against Heracles by hanging her from the sky with golden bonds and anvils tied to her feet. Hephaestus was thrown from Olympus by Zeus for trying to help her.

**Leto and Delos**
Out of jealousy, Hera forbade Leto, pregnant with Apollo and Artemis by Zeus, from giving birth on any land. Leto finally gave birth on the floating island of Delos.

**Boopis and the spring of Canathus**
Homer's epithet for Hera is boopis, "cow-eyed." She bathed every year in the spring of Canathus near Nauplia to renew her virginity.
